000|exhaustive.md:
Happy to help. Since I don't know which class this is for, how much time is left, or what kind of questions it will ask, I'll lay out a plan that holds up across most subjects. Skip whatever doesn't apply.

### First, pin down what is actually being tested

Before you study anything, spend ten minutes collecting:

- The review sheet or study guide, if your teacher handed one out. If one exists, it outranks everything else here.
- The syllabus or unit outline, which usually lists topics in the order they were taught and therefore the order they'll be assessed.
- Old quizzes, homework, and labs from the unit. Teachers reuse question *types* far more faithfully than they reuse questions.
- Anything your teacher said twice or circled on the board. Repetition in class signals weighting.

If none of that exists, ask directly: how many questions, what format (multiple choice, short answer, essay, problems), and which chapters or units.

### Work backward from the date

- **More than a week out:** short sessions across several days beat one long block. **Spaced practice** using the same total hours spread over more days produces noticeably better retention than the equivalent single sitting.
- **Two or three days out:** assign one topic per session and take the hardest one first, while you're fresh.
- **The night before:** do not learn new material. Review, quiz yourself, sleep.

### Study by testing yourself, not by rereading

Rereading notes feels productive because the material starts to look familiar, but familiarity is not the same skill as producing an answer on a blank page under time pressure. The methods that actually move scores:

- **Active recall.** Close the book, write down everything you can about a topic, then check what you missed. What you missed is your real study list.
- **Practice questions.** Work them under something close to test conditions, then grade yourself honestly.
- **Explaining out loud.** Teach the topic to a friend or an empty room. Wherever you stall is a gap you'd never notice while reading.
- **Flashcards,** but only for material that is genuinely memorization: vocabulary, dates, formulas, definitions.

### Adjust for the kind of test it is

- **Math or physics:** redo problems you got wrong, without looking at the worked solution first. Reading someone else's solution builds recognition, not ability.
- **History or social studies:** build a rough timeline, then practice explaining causes and consequences rather than reciting isolated dates.
- **A science with processes and diagrams:** be able to draw the diagram from memory, label it, and say what happens at each step and why it happens in that order.
- **A foreign language:** drill vocabulary in both directions and practice producing sentences, not just recognizing them.
- **Literature:** know two or three quotations well enough to actually use, and be ready to argue a position rather than retell the plot.
- **Any essay test:** outline two likely prompts in advance. You're graded on structure nearly as much as on content.

### The last twenty-four hours

- Sleep a full night. Sleep does more for recall than the extra hour of cramming costs you.
- Eat something beforehand. Low blood sugar looks exactly like not knowing the material.
- Pack what you need the night before: calculator, pencils, charged batteries, formula sheet if one is allowed.
- Get there early enough that you aren't starting the test out of breath.

### During the test

Read the whole thing before answering. Take what you know first and mark what you don't. Watch point values against the clock so a four-percent question doesn't eat a quarter of the period, and if there's no guessing penalty, leave nothing blank.

### How to tell you're ready

You're ready when you can, with your notes closed, list the major topics, define the key terms for each, and work one representative question from each without help.

All of that is deliberately general, and general advice is the least efficient kind. Which class is this for, how many days do you have, and is it multiple choice or writing? With those three answers I can turn this into an actual plan.
000|exhaustive.note: With every lever off it produces a defensible, thorough study plan for no particular test, and has to close by asking for the subject the context lever would have supplied.

Coming back to a class you've been away from is a different job from ordinary review, so I'll start further back than you might expect and define things as they come up. Skip anything that's already familiar.

Start with the **syllabus**, the document handed out at the beginning of the term that lists what the course covers and roughly when. It is usually the fastest way to reconstruct what the units were. Alongside it there may be a **study guide** or **review sheet**, a shorter document written for this specific test that says which topics are fair game. If a review sheet exists, it is the single most valuable object you can get hold of, and it is worth emailing your teacher tonight to ask whether there is one.

Next, find the textbook chapters matching those units. Most textbooks end each chapter with a summary and a set of review questions. The summary tells you what the chapter considered important; the review questions show you what a test question about it tends to look like. Read all of the summaries first, before you read any full chapter. That gives you a map of the territory instead of a close-up of one corner of it.

A few words you'll run into while studying, defined:

- **Key terms:** the bolded vocabulary in the textbook. On most tests a real fraction of the available points come from being able to define these on demand.
- **Active recall:** trying to produce an answer from memory before checking it. This is the difference between studying and reading.
- **Flashcards:** a prompt on one side, the answer on the other, paper or app. Good for definitions and facts, poor for anything requiring reasoning.
- **Practice test:** any set of questions you answer under test-like conditions and then grade.
- **Cramming:** compressing all your studying into one session immediately before the test. It works passably for facts and badly for anything you have to work through.

Because you missed this material rather than forgot it, prioritize breadth over depth. A rough working grasp of every topic scores better than mastery of one topic and blankness on the rest. Go down the topic list and mark each one "could explain it," "have heard of it," or "no idea." Spend tonight on the middle group. Those are cheap points. The "no idea" pile is expensive and should come last.

Then talk to the teacher, in person if you can. Say plainly that you were out and ask what they would focus on. Most teachers will tell you, and some will tell you a great deal.

One thing I can't do from here is tell you what to read. What class is this for, and how long until the test? With that I could point you at the actual topics instead of the process for finding them.

000|dense.md:
There is a version of test preparation that works for nearly any subject, and it's worth starting on before we narrow anything down. The first move is always to establish what is actually being assessed, because most wasted studying is time spent on material that was never going to appear: dig out the review sheet if one exists, the syllabus or unit outline if it doesn't, and every quiz, homework set, and lab from the unit, since teachers reuse question types much more faithfully than they reuse questions. Once you know the scope, break it into topics and sort them by how confident you feel rather than by the order they were taught, then plan to spend most of your remaining time on the ones sitting in the middle of that list, where a small amount of work converts directly into points. From there, the single most reliable change available to most people is to stop rereading. Rereading notes produces a powerful sense of familiarity that has very little to do with whether you can generate an answer when the page in front of you is blank, and the correction is to close the book and write out what you know, or work a problem without glancing at the solution, or explain the topic aloud to somebody who will interrupt whenever you skip a step. Whatever falls out of that process is your genuine study list.

Spread the work over as many sittings as the calendar still allows rather than one long push, because the same two hours split across three evenings holds better than two hours the night before; if one night is all there is, spend it on review and self-quizzing rather than on new material, which tends to produce confident wrong answers. Sleep is worth more than the hour of cramming it costs, as is eating beforehand and arriving early enough to catch your breath. In the room itself, read all the way through before answering, take what you know first, mark what you don't and come back to it, and keep an eye on point values so a four-point question doesn't eat a third of the period. That is all sound and none of it is aimed at you in particular, which is the limitation of answering before I know anything: what subject is the test in, when is it, and what kind of questions does it ask? Those three answers would let me tell you what to do tonight rather than how to decide.

100|exhaustive.md:
Two hours tonight and a test Friday means you can cover all three of Mr. Dalton's topics rather than only the one that burned you, and come back to the mitosis stages at the end. Here's what this unit usually asks about, plus a fix for the metaphase and anaphase problem.

### Cell structure

You'll almost certainly have to know the main parts and what each one does:

- The **cell membrane** is the outer boundary. It controls what gets in and out.
- The **nucleus** holds the DNA and directs the cell's activity.
- **Mitochondria** release usable energy from food.
- **Ribosomes** build proteins.
- The **endoplasmic reticulum** is a folded network that moves material around the cell. The rough kind has ribosomes stuck to it; the smooth kind doesn't.
- The **Golgi apparatus** packages proteins and ships them out.
- **Lysosomes** break down waste and worn-out parts.
- The **cytoplasm** is the fluid everything sits in.
- Plant cells also have a stiff **cell wall**, **chloroplasts** for photosynthesis, and one large **vacuole** that stores material and keeps the plant firm.

Two question shapes are almost guaranteed: a plant-versus-animal comparison, and being handed a job ("makes proteins") and asked which part does it. Practice both directions. You may also get asked about bacteria, which lack a nucleus along with most of the other compartments.

### Osmosis and diffusion

Diffusion is spreading out. Anything dissolved drifts from where there's a lot of it toward where there's less, until it's even. It costs the cell nothing. Perfume filling a room is the standard illustration.

Osmosis is the same idea, except it's the water doing the moving and it's crossing the cell membrane. The rule to hold onto is that water moves toward the saltier side. If the liquid outside the cell has more dissolved in it than the inside does, water leaves and the cell shrinks. If the outside is plainer than the inside, water comes in and the cell swells, and an animal cell without a wall can burst. If the two match, water still crosses both ways but nothing changes overall.

Mr. Dalton will very likely draw a beaker with a cell in it and ask which way the water goes. Decide which side has more dissolved material, then send the water that way.

Some materials get moved the opposite direction, from where there's less toward where there's more, and doing that costs the cell energy. Watch for questions that turn on whether energy is required, because that's the whole point of them.

### The stages of mitosis

Mitosis is one cell dividing into two identical cells. Before it starts, the DNA has already been copied. The order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, and then the body of the cell itself splits.

- **Prophase:** the copied DNA coils up into chromosomes you can actually see, the wrapper around the nucleus comes apart, and fibers start reaching in from both ends of the cell.
- **Metaphase:** the chromosomes line up in one row across the center.
- **Anaphase:** the two halves of each chromosome are pulled apart toward opposite ends.
- **Telophase:** two new nuclei form around the two groups, and the chromosomes uncoil again.

For the pair you keep swapping, use the first letters. **M**etaphase is **m**iddle. **A**naphase is **a**part. Middle comes before apart in the alphabet and in the cell, so the mnemonic hands you the order as well as the events. If you can say that sentence Friday, those questions are yours.

It's also worth knowing that the long stretch before mitosis, when the cell grows and copies its DNA, is called interphase, and that it is not one of the mitosis stages even though it appears in most diagrams. That's a classic trick question.

Any picture of a cell caught mid-division is asking you where the chromosomes are: still lined up in the center, being dragged toward the ends, or clumped at the two poles with new nuclei forming.

If you want a way to choose between these tonight, check which of the three Mr. Dalton spent the most class time on. That's usually what the test weights heaviest.

Since Friday's test covers the whole cell unit, the safest use of tonight is a rebuild rather than a review, so nothing below assumes you held onto anything from earlier in the term. I'll define each word before using it.

A **cell** is the smallest unit of a living thing, and everything alive is made of one or more. A cell is not a solid lump. It's a bag of watery fluid with structures floating in it, and the bag has a boundary called the **cell membrane** that holds it together and decides what passes through.

The fluid inside is **cytoplasm**. The structures floating in it are **organelles**, a word that just means "little organs," and each has one job. The **nucleus** is the control center and stores the instructions. **Mitochondria** turn food into energy the cell can spend. **Ribosomes** build proteins, which are the molecules that do most of the actual work. Plant cells have three things animal cells don't: a rigid **cell wall** outside the membrane, green **chloroplasts** that make food from sunlight, and a large **vacuole** that stores water and holds the cell's shape.

That covers the first of Mr. Dalton's three topics. The second is movement across that membrane. **Diffusion** is the word for particles spreading from a crowded area into a less crowded one, the way a smell fills a room without anyone fanning it. **Osmosis** is that same spreading when the thing moving is water and it's crossing the cell membrane. Because the membrane lets water through much more easily than it lets dissolved material through, the water is what ends up moving, and it moves toward whichever side has more dissolved in it. That single sentence is most of the topic, and most test questions on it are that sentence applied to a drawing.

The third topic is division. The instructions in the nucleus are stored in a molecule called **DNA**. When a cell prepares to divide, the DNA is copied and coils into short thick packages called **chromosomes**, which is why they become visible under a microscope at that point and not before. **Mitosis** is the process of one cell becoming two cells with identical instructions, and it runs through four named stages in a fixed order. **Prophase** is when the chromosomes become visible and the nucleus's wrapper breaks apart. **Metaphase** is when the chromosomes line up in a single row across the center of the cell. **Anaphase** is when each chromosome is pulled into two halves that travel toward opposite ends. **Telophase** is when two new nuclei form and the chromosomes unwind. After that, the cell body itself divides in two.

If you can define cell, membrane, cytoplasm, organelle, diffusion, osmosis, chromosome, and mitosis without looking, and then recite those four stages in order, you'll have the foundation the rest of Mr. Dalton's questions are built on top of.

Given that Friday is the deadline and tonight is the block you actually have, I'd put the mitosis stages first while you're fresh, since that's the part that cost you points last time, and let cell structure ride on whatever you already know. What makes metaphase and anaphase blur together is that both descriptions involve chromosomes doing something near the center of the cell, so what you want is a difference you can see in a picture rather than a phrase you have to remember: in metaphase the chromosomes are still whole and parked in one neat row across the middle, while in anaphase they have already been split, with one half of each traveling toward each end, which artists usually draw as a scatter of small V shapes instead of a line. Osmosis and diffusion come down to one sentence you can carry into the room with you, which is that water moves toward whichever side has more stuff dissolved in it. Saltier outside, the cell shrinks; plainer outside, the cell swells; the same on both sides, nothing changes on net. Diffusion is that same drift but for the dissolved material rather than the water, and it doesn't cost the cell anything, which is usually the actual thing a question is checking. 001|exhaustive.md:
Point loss here concentrates in three places, and in each case it comes from one discrimination collapsing under pressure. What follows works through all three, with recall prompts closing each block; answer those aloud before looking back.

### Tonicity and the direction of net water movement

Tonicity is not a property a solution has on its own; it is a statement about a solution relative to the interior of a particular cell, and it concerns only non-penetrating solutes, the ones the membrane refuses to pass. Osmolarity counts every dissolved particle regardless of whether it can cross, so two solutions of identical osmolarity can differ in tonicity. A urea solution isosmotic to plasma is functionally hypotonic to a red blood cell: the urea equilibrates, water follows it in, and the cell swells.

Water moves toward the compartment holding the greater effective solute concentration, or equivalently from higher to lower water potential.

The outcomes get asked as a matched set:

- Hypertonic outside: net efflux. An animal cell shrinks into the scalloped outline called crenation; a plant cell's protoplast pulls away from the wall, which is plasmolysis.
- Hypotonic outside: net influx. An animal cell swells and may burst; a plant cell swells against its wall and develops turgor pressure, its normal working state rather than a failure.
- Isotonic outside: no net volume change, though water keeps crossing both ways at equal rates.

Aquaporins, dedicated water channels, govern the rate rather than the direction; a question describing unusually fast volume change is testing those.

Recall prompts: give the fate of an animal cell and a plant cell in all three tonicities, and explain why matching osmolarity does not guarantee isotonicity.

### Passive versus active transport

The discrimination that costs most here is not "is a protein involved." Facilitated diffusion uses channel proteins and carrier proteins and remains passive, because the solute descends its electrochemical gradient and the cell spends nothing. The classification question is directional: down the gradient or up it?

Passive: simple diffusion of small nonpolar species straight through the phospholipid bilayer, facilitated diffusion through channels or carriers, and osmosis, the special case where the mobile species is water.

Active transport moves against the gradient at metabolic cost. Primary active transport couples that movement directly to ATP hydrolysis at the transporter, the sodium-potassium pump being the standard case at three sodium out for two potassium in. Secondary active transport spends none itself: it lets sodium fall back down the gradient the pump established and couples that descent to a second solute climbing, alongside it in a symport or opposite it in an antiport. It remains energy-dependent one step removed, which is why a metabolic poison stops it too.

Recall prompts: given internal and external concentrations plus a note on ATP availability, classify each movement, and explain why a poison blocking ATP synthesis halts intestinal glucose uptake but not alveolar oxygen uptake.

### Chromosome behavior phase by phase

Replication occurs in S phase, within interphase. A cell entering prophase already carries each chromosome as two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, and holding that fact steady prevents most of the errors below.

- Prophase: chromatin condenses, the nucleolus disperses, and the mitotic spindle organizes from the centrosomes. The nuclear envelope fragments, and kinetochores assemble on each centromere and capture spindle microtubules.
- Metaphase: chromosomes are aligned at the metaphase plate, each attached to both poles and each still a joined pair of chromatids under balanced bipolar tension.
- Anaphase: cohesin is cleaved, the chromatids separate, and each becomes an independent chromosome traveling poleward. Chromosome number transiently doubles.
- Telophase: nuclear envelopes reassemble, chromosomes decondense, the spindle disassembles. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm, by cleavage furrow in animals and cell plate in plants.

The cue that separates the pair people invert: ask whether the centromeres are still holding partners together, not whether the chromosomes look aligned. Alignment proves nothing, since anaphase begins from an aligned plate. Joined pairs in one plane is metaphase; separated singles in transit, usually V-shaped with the centromere leading, is anaphase.

Recall prompts: sketch a four-chromosome cell at metaphase and at anaphase and write the chromatid count beside each; say what one unattached kinetochore does to the timing.

Each of these three areas sits on a small vocabulary, and none of the reasoning works until those words are solid, so here they are in dependency order. Nothing below assumes you have met any of it.

Two words first. A **solute** is anything dissolved in a liquid: salt, sugar, ions. A **concentration gradient** is simply a difference in the amount of a solute between two places. A membrane is **semipermeable** when it allows some substances across and blocks others; a cell's membrane is semipermeable, and critically it stops most solutes while letting water through.

Given those, **osmosis** is the movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from the side holding less solute to the side holding more. **Tonicity** is the vocabulary used to describe which side that is. A surrounding solution is *hypotonic* when it holds less solute than the cell's interior, so water enters and the cell swells; an animal cell, having no wall to push back, can **lyse**, meaning rupture. It is *hypertonic* when it holds more, so water exits and the cell shrivels. It is **isotonic** when the two are equal and there is no net movement. In a plant cell, incoming water presses the contents against a rigid outer **cell wall** and produces **turgor pressure**, which is what makes a stem stand up instead of wilting.

Next, transport, which means anything crossing that membrane. Movement costing the cell no energy is called *passive*. It includes **simple diffusion**, particles crossing on their own, and **facilitated diffusion**, in which a **channel protein** (a pore through the membrane) or a **carrier protein** (a shuttle that changes shape) assists a molecule across without pushing it. Both are passive because the substance is already traveling in the direction the gradient favors. Movement costing energy is *active transport*: the cell spends **ATP**, the molecule it uses as energy currency, to force something the wrong way along its gradient. The standard example is the **sodium-potassium pump**, which drives sodium out and potassium in, both uphill.

Last, division. **DNA** is the molecule holding the cell's instructions. Before a cell divides, its DNA is copied, and each copy winds into a rod called a **chromatid**; the two identical chromatids belonging to one chromosome remain fastened at a pinched point called the **centromere**. **Mitosis**, the division of one cell into two identical cells, then proceeds through four stages: prophase, in which the chromosomes condense, the **nuclear envelope** around the DNA disassembles, and **spindle fibers** grow from opposite ends of the cell; metaphase, in which the chromosomes align in one plane across the middle; anaphase, in which the centromeres release and the paired chromatids are hauled to opposite poles; and telophase, in which nuclear envelopes re-form and the chromosomes unwind. **Cytokinesis**, the splitting of the cell body itself, finishes the job.

Recall prompts, worth more than rereading: define solute, tonicity, and centromere without looking; give the direction water travels for a cell placed in a saltier bath; say which stage still has chromatids fastened together.

001|dense.md:
Everything in these three areas reduces to one question asked three different ways: which direction, and at whose expense. For water the direction is always toward the greater concentration of non-penetrating solute, so a cell in a saltier bath loses volume and an animal cell takes on the scalloped profile called crenation while a walled plant cell undergoes plasmolysis as its protoplast peels inward, and a cell in a more dilute bath gains volume, which for a red blood cell ends in hemolysis and for a plant cell ends in the ordinary turgor pressure that holds tissue upright; when the two are isotonic the volume simply holds steady, which is not the same claim as the traffic stopping. The distinction most often missed here is that tonicity and osmolarity are different measurements, the first counting only particles the membrane will not pass, which is why a urea solution matched to plasma by osmolarity will still burst a cell.

For solutes rather than water, the same directional question becomes whether movement follows the electrochemical gradient or opposes it, and the trap is reading the presence of a protein as evidence of expenditure: facilitated diffusion through a channel protein or a carrier protein is entirely passive and costs nothing, whereas primary active transport hydrolyzes ATP at the transporter itself, the sodium-potassium pump being the canonical case at three sodium out for two potassium in, and secondary active transport pays indirectly by letting sodium run back down the gradient the pump built and coupling that descent to a second solute being hauled uphill, riding with it in a symporter or facing it in an antiporter. For chromosomes the direction is poleward or not, and the discriminating feature is the centromere, not the alignment: through prophase and metaphase each chromosome persists as two sister chromatids fastened together, arranged in single file at the metaphase plate with kinetochores under equal tension from both poles, and only when cohesin is cleaved at anaphase onset do those chromatids part and travel outward as full chromosomes, which is why the count transiently doubles. Alignment identifies nothing, since anaphase begins from an aligned plate; the number of attached partners identifies it at once. Rather than rereading any of this, close it and try to produce from memory what becomes of a walled cell and an unwalled one in each tonicity, one passive and one active example moving the same ion, and a labeled sketch of four chromosomes at each of the two phases with the chromatid number beside it.

101|exhaustive.md:
The metaphase and anaphase confusion is the most fixable thing on your list, because the two phases differ by one structural fact rather than by appearance. I'll take that first and then work through all three of Mr. Dalton's topics at the level this unit gets tested.

### The cue that separates the pair

Do not use "lined up in the middle." Anaphase begins from a lined-up plate, and a good fraction of textbook diagrams are drawn partway through the transition, so alignment is not evidence. Use the centromere.

- Metaphase: every chromosome is still two sister chromatids fastened at a centromere, sitting at the metaphase plate, with kinetochores on both faces of that centromere pulled by microtubules from opposite poles of the mitotic spindle. The tension is balanced in both directions, which is precisely why they stall in a plane instead of drifting.
- Anaphase: cohesin, the protein ring clamping the chromatids together, has been cleaved. Each former chromatid is now a chromosome in its own right, moving poleward, usually drawn as a V with the centromere leading and the arms trailing behind it.

Attached is metaphase; released is anaphase. Test it now: draw a cell with four chromosomes at each phase and write the chromatid count and the chromosome count beside each. If those came out identical, that is the misconception underneath the quiz, and repairing it repairs every phase question at once.

### The rest of the sequence

Interphase is not a stage of mitosis, and that gets tested. Replication happens in S phase inside interphase, which is why a cell entering prophase already has paired chromatids.

Prophase: chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, the nucleolus disperses, and the spindle organizes from centrosomes at opposite ends. The nuclear envelope fragments, and kinetochores capture spindle microtubules.

Telophase: nuclear envelopes reassemble around each set, chromosomes decondense, the spindle takes itself apart.

Cytokinesis: a cleavage furrow pinches an animal cell in two, while a plant cell builds a cell plate instead, because a wall cannot be pinched. That contrast appears constantly and it is free points.

Ask yourself, without looking: what is present at metaphase that is absent at telophase, and what is present at both?

### Osmosis and diffusion, and where the direction questions fail

Water moves toward the side holding more non-penetrating solute; say it as "water chases solute" and you will not invert it under pressure. Hypertonic outside means net efflux, so an animal cell shrivels into crenation and a plant cell undergoes plasmolysis as the contents peel off the wall. Hypotonic outside means net influx: an animal cell swells and may burst, while a plant cell becomes turgid and gains turgor pressure, which is healthy rather than damaged. Isotonic means equal fluxes, not halted fluxes, which is a favorite trick.

For the harder questions: tonicity is not osmolarity. Osmolarity counts all dissolved particles; tonicity counts only those that cannot cross. Aquaporins are the dedicated channels that make water crossing fast.

Retrieval: for each tonicity, state what happens to a red blood cell and to a root hair cell, and which survives the hypotonic case.

### Transport

The error that costs the most points here is treating "a protein is involved" as evidence of active transport. Facilitated diffusion moves solutes through channel proteins or carrier proteins and is passive, because the solute is descending its electrochemical gradient and the cell pays nothing. Active transport is defined by direction: uphill, against the gradient, at a cost. The sodium-potassium pump hydrolyzes ATP directly and moves three sodium out for two potassium in. Secondary active transport runs on the sodium gradient that pump created rather than on ATP itself, which still makes it energy-dependent one step back.

One question settles nearly every classification item: which way is the solute going relative to its own gradient?

### Cell structure

Know each organelle by function and run the question backward, so that "packages and ships proteins" produces Golgi. The plant-versus-animal comparison, meaning cell wall, chloroplasts, and the large central vacuole, is close to guaranteed. Give membrane structure a look too, since selective permeability is what every transport question above rests on.

A wrong answer about a phase is usually a wrong answer about a chromosome one layer down, so rather than starting where you think the problem is, I'll start at the definitions and build forward until Friday's material arrives on top of them. Every term is defined before it gets used.

A **cell** is the smallest unit that qualifies as alive. Its boundary is the **plasma membrane**, a double sheet of fat molecules called a **phospholipid bilayer**, and that sheet is **selectively permeable**, meaning some substances cross it freely while others cannot cross at all. The watery fluid inside is the **cytosol**, and suspended in it are **organelles**, small compartments each performing one job: the **nucleus** stores the instructions, **mitochondria** release usable energy, **ribosomes** assemble proteins.

Two more definitions before the second topic. A **solute** is any substance dissolved in a liquid. A **concentration gradient** is a difference in the amount of a solute between two regions. **Diffusion** is the net movement of a solute from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration, and it is *passive*, meaning the cell spends nothing on it. **Osmosis** is that same process applied to water crossing a selectively permeable membrane, and the net direction is always into whichever compartment holds more solute. The vocabulary for the comparison: *hypertonic* means the outside solution holds more solute than the cell does, so water leaves; *hypotonic* means it holds less, so water enters; **isotonic** means neither, so volume stays put. In a plant cell, entering water presses outward against the wall and generates **turgor pressure**.

When a cell spends **ATP**, the molecule it uses as energy currency, to move a substance against its gradient, that is *active transport*, and the **sodium-potassium pump** is the standard example. When a protein merely helps a substance travel the way its gradient already sends it, that is **facilitated diffusion**, which is still passive.

Now division. Instructions are stored in **DNA**, which in a resting cell exists as loose threads called **chromatin**. Before division the DNA is copied and the chromatin coils into compact **chromosomes**. Each copied chromosome consists of two identical halves, each one a **chromatid**, joined at a narrow waist called the **centromere**. **Mitosis** is division producing two identical cells, in four named stages. In **prophase**, the chromosomes condense into view, the **nuclear envelope** breaks apart, and **spindle fibers** extend inward from the poles. In *metaphase*, the chromosomes line up along the middle of the cell. In *anaphase*, the centromeres release and the chromatids travel to opposite poles. In **telophase**, nuclear envelopes re-form and the chromosomes unwind. **Cytokinesis**, the division of the cell body, completes the process.

Say each bolded definition aloud before Friday, and the rest of Mr. Dalton's questions will have somewhere to land.

101|dense.md:
Start with the two stages you keep swapping, because the confusion has one cause and naming it ends it. Both stages put chromosomes near the center of the cell, so "lined up in the middle" decides nothing, particularly since anaphase begins from an aligned plate and many diagrams are drawn mid-transition. What separates them is whether the halves are still fastened: throughout metaphase every chromosome is a pair of identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere, resting at the metaphase plate with kinetochores on either face held under equal tension by microtubules from both spindle poles, whereas anaphase is defined by the cleavage of the cohesin ring binding that pair, after which each chromatid is a chromosome in its own right and is hauled outward, so the only thing to ask of a diagram is whether a given chromosome still has its partner attached at the centromere, a yes putting you in metaphase and a no in anaphase. It also explains the shape, since anaphase is usually pictured as a scatter of V forms whose bend points toward the pole each is heading for. Prove it by drawing four chromosomes in each phase and writing the chromatid count beside each; if those counts come out equal, that is the misconception the last quiz found, and exactly what Mr. Dalton's diagram questions are built to catch.

The other two topics reward the same habit of asking about direction rather than appearance. Water travels toward the side holding more solute that cannot cross the membrane, so a hypertonic surrounding pulls water out and an animal cell shrivels into crenation while a plant cell undergoes plasmolysis as its contents peel away from the wall, and a hypotonic surrounding drives water in, bursting an animal cell but only making a plant cell turgid with the turgor pressure that keeps it standing; isotonic surroundings leave volume unchanged though molecules keep crossing both ways. For solutes rather than water, the mistake to avoid is reading a helper protein as proof that energy was spent, since facilitated diffusion through a channel protein or carrier protein costs nothing and merely follows the electrochemical gradient, whereas active transport is defined by climbing against that gradient at the price of ATP, as the sodium-potassium pump does in sending three sodium out for two potassium in. Cell structure sits underneath all of this, since the phospholipid bilayer is why some things cross unaided while others need a pump, and organelle function questions remain the cheapest points in the unit.
